ethiopia.title: Ethiopia Turns COP31 Diplomacy Into Strategic Opportunity to Advance COP32 and Africa's Climate Agenda
ethiopia.content: Africa: Ethiopia Turns COP31 Diplomacy Into Strategic Opportunity to Advance COP32 and Africa's Climate Agenda - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Africa: Ethiopia Turns COP31 Diplomacy Into Strategic Opportunity to Advance COP32 and Africa's Climate Agenda 15 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) By Staff Writer November 15 , 2026 (ENA) By hosting COP32 in 2027, Ethiopia seeks to translate its growing diplomatic influence into climate investment, green development partnerships and stronger African representation in global climate negotiations. Ethiopia's preparations to host the 32nd United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP32) in Addis Ababa in November 2027 are already taking shape on the diplomatic stage, with the country using the ongoing COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, to build partnerships, advance Africa's climate priorities and lay the groundwork for an ambitious global conference. For Ethiopia, COP32 represents far more than the responsibility of hosting one of the world's most consequential international gatherings. It offers a strategic opportunity to strengthen the country's diplomatic standing, mobilize climate finance, attract investment, showcase its green development initiatives and position Africa more prominently in international climate negotiations. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines The diplomatic push underway at COP31 is therefore particularly significant. Through high-level engagements with the current COP Presidency, negotiating groups and international partners, Ethiopia is seeking to ensure that the transition towards COP32 begins with a clear agenda: turning climate commitments into practical action, making climate finance more accessible and connecting environmental protection with economic transformation. At the heart of this ambition is a development philosophy that views climate action not as a separate environmental undertaking but as an essential pillar of economic policy. Addressing the opening of COP31 in Antalya, Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed captured this approach in a clear message: "In Ethiopia, climate action is economic policy." The Prime Minister explained that changing weather patterns have direct consequences for agricultural production, electricity generation, livelihoods and the country's broader development trajectory. Droughts and floods associated with El Niño, he noted, can disrupt harvests, displace families and impose prolonged economic costs. "The rain comes back, floods subside, but recovery takes much longer," he observed. His remarks underscore why climate resilience has become increasingly central to Ethiopia's development priorities. For a country whose economy remains closely connected to agriculture and hydropower, climate-related disruptions are not simply environmental challenges; they threaten productivity, economic stability and the livelihoods of millions. This perspective is expected to inform Ethiopia's preparations for COP32, particularly its emphasis on adaptation, early-warning systems, climate finance and investment in resilient infrastructure. From COP31 diplomatic engagement to COP32 leadership The arrival of Foreign Affairs Minister and COP32 President-Designate Gedion Timothewos in Antalya to participate in COP31 marks an important phase in Ethiopia's diplomatic preparations. His engagements with the current COP Presidency, negotiating groups and international partners are expected to help establish the political and institutional foundations for a successful conference in Addis Ababa. Ethiopia has expressed its ambition to make COP32 inclusive, action-oriented and implementation-focused, with particular attention to the needs of developing countries. The objective is to move beyond repeated declarations and ensure that international climate commitments translate into accessible financing, technology partnerships and tangible outcomes. The country's selection as host reflects both its diplomatic standing and Africa's collective ambition to secure a stronger voice in shaping global climate policy. The African Group of Negotiators unanimously endorsed Ethiopia's candidacy during COP30 in Belém, Brazil, in November 2025. Although Nigeria initially competed for the hosting opportunity, it eventually stepped aside, allowing Africa to present a unified position. The UNFCCC subsequently accepted Ethiopia's offer to host COP32 in Addis Ababa from November 8 to 19, 2027. Several factors underpin Ethiopia's selection. Addis Ababa, as the headquarters of the African Union (AU) and a major center of international diplomacy, provides an important institutional advantage. Hosting COP32 will create an opportunity to connect global climate negotiations with continental development priorities and strengthen cooperation between African institutions and international partners. Ethiopia has also demonstrated its capacity to convene major international climate discussions. In September 2025, the country hosted the Second Africa Climate Summit, bringing together more than 26,000 participants and producing the Addis Ababa Declaration on Climate Change and Call for Action. The summit provided an important platform for advancing African-led climate finance, innovation and collective action. Its outcomes also established a foundation upon which Ethiopia can build as it prepares to host the global climate conference. Equally important are the country's domestic green development initiatives, including the Climate-Resilient Green Economy Strategy, the Green Legacy Initiative and substantial investments in renewable energy. Together, these initiatives provide Ethiopia with practical experiences to bring into international discussions on how developing countries can pursue economic growth while protecting natural resources and building resilience against climate change. COP32: An opportunity to advance Africa's climate priorities Beyond its national diplomatic and economic interests, Ethiopia's hosting of COP32 carries considerable continental significance. Africa contributes a relatively small share of global greenhouse gas emissions but faces some of the most severe consequences of climate change. Prolonged droughts, devastating floods, land degradation, food insecurity and water stress continue to threaten communities and undermine development gains across the continent. Yet African countries face persistent challenges in accessing affordable climate finance, transferring advanced technologies and building the institutional capacity needed to respond effectively. For this reason, climate finance, adaptation, technology transfer and capacity building remain central to Africa's negotiating priorities. Ethiopia's selection as host therefore represents an opportunity to strengthen the continent's collective negotiating position and ensure that its development concerns receive greater attention in international climate decision-making. The conference could also help advance African-led initiatives, including the proposed Africa Climate Innovation Compact and African Climate Facility, aimed at mobilizing resources and supporting climate solutions across the continent. The broader objective is to move beyond presenting Africa primarily as a continent vulnerable to climate change and increasingly recognize its potential as a source of renewable energy, environmental solutions, innovation and sustainable investment opportunities. Mobilizing climate finance for sustainable development One of the most significant opportunities presented by COP32 is the potential to mobilize climate finance and attract investment into Ethiopia's green economy. The country requires substantial resources to expand renewable energy, modernize agriculture, develop irrigation, restore degraded landscapes and build climate-resilient infrastructure. Its dependence on rain-fed agriculture and hydropower also makes it particularly vulnerable to changing rainfall patterns, prolonged droughts and extreme weather events. Against this backdrop, COP32 could provide a major platform for engaging multilateral climate funds, development banks, bilateral partners and private investors. Such partnerships could support investments in renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, water infrastructure, forest restoration, climate-resilient cities and disaster preparedness. However, attracting international attention alone will not be sufficient. Ethiopia's ability to translate diplomatic engagement into investment-ready projects, affordable financing and sustainable development partnerships will be critical to realizing the conference's potential. Prime Minister Abiy has particularly emphasized the importance of predictable and accessible climate finance, arguing that resources must reach vulnerable communities before disasters cause widespread damage. Outlining the approach Ethiopia intends to advance at COP32, he said: "We will put early action at the center, funding released when warning comes, reaching the most exposed first." This vision points to an important shift in global climate policy: moving from financing recovery after disasters towards investing in preparedness, prevention and resilience before they occur. For developing countries, timely access to climate finance, reliable forecasting and effective early-warning systems can protect agricultural production, infrastructure and vulnerable communities while reducing the enormous economic costs of climate-related disasters. Making this approach a practical outcome of COP32 could give Ethiopia an opportunity to contribute to a more responsive and development-oriented international climate finance system. Renewable energy: Connecting green development with regional economic integration Renewable energy is another major area in which Ethiopia can demonstrate the relationship between climate action and economic transformation. The country possesses considerable hydropower, wind, solar and geothermal resources, offering significant potential to expand clean electricity generation, support industrialization and strengthen regional energy cooperation. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), alongside other renewable energy investments, illustrates Ethiopia's ambition to expand domestic electricity generation and enhance its role in regional power integration. Addressing COP31, Prime Minister Abiy highlighted the regional importance of Ethiopia's hydropower resources, noting that more than 90 percent of the country's electricity comes from water, including electricity supplied to neighboring countries. This demonstrates that Ethiopia's renewable energy investments have implications beyond its national borders. Expanded electricity generation and cross-border power trade can support regional industrial development, improve energy access and strengthen economic interdependence. Through COP32, Ethiopia could attract partnerships and investment in energy storage, transmission infrastructure, renewable energy technologies and regional electricity markets. Such investments would help accelerate industrialization, expand electricity access and strengthen the country's position as an emerging regional electricity supplier. At the same time, the Prime Minister acknowledged the importance of diversifying the country's energy mix to reduce vulnerability to changing rainfall patterns and fluctuations in water availability. "We are also taking a long view with our energy supply, developing wind, solar, and geothermal power, while planning for nuclear, so a dry year does less harm to our economy," he said. The strategy reflects the importance of a diversified and reliable energy supply in supporting economic expansion. While hydropower remains central to Ethiopia's electricity generation, developing alternative energy sources can strengthen resilience against drought and improve long-term energy security. Protecting agriculture and safeguarding Ethiopia's global coffee heritage Climate resilience is equally important to Ethiopia's agricultural transformation. Erratic rainfall, prolonged droughts, flooding and land degradation continue to threaten agricultural productivity and rural livelihoods. Strengthening the sector's resilience therefore requires investment in irrigation, improved seeds, soil conservation, agricultural research, climate information services and early-warning systems. At COP31, Prime Minister Abiy highlighted the role of emerging technologies in strengthening climate monitoring and helping farmers respond to changing weather conditions. "We use satellite data to watch the land, and we are improving forecasts with artificial intelligence to give farmers earlier warning," he said. The application of satellite monitoring, artificial intelligence and advanced forecasting systems could help farmers anticipate extreme weather events, make better-informed planting and harvesting decisions and minimize agricultural losses. Ethiopia could use COP32 to advocate for greater international cooperation in climate information systems, technology transfer and capacity building, particularly for countries with limited resources to develop these capabilities independently. The issue also has implications for Ethiopia's international trade and global agricultural reputation. Drawing attention to the climate threats facing one of the country's most celebrated exports, the Prime Minister noted that changing temperatures and rainfall patterns are endangering the forests and farms where Ethiopian Arabica coffee is grown. "Many of you begin your day with Ethiopia's gift to the world, Arabica coffee, but rising temperatures and changing rainfall threaten the forests and the farms where it grows," he stated. The message connects climate change with livelihoods, export earnings and global agricultural value chains. Ethiopia's coffee sector, deeply rooted in the country's natural forests and agricultural communities, illustrates how environmental degradation can affect both domestic economic interests and international markets. Protecting coffee-growing landscapes, strengthening agricultural adaptation and supporting sustainable production are therefore not merely environmental priorities. They are essential to safeguarding an important source of export revenue and the livelihoods of farming communities. For Ethiopia, COP32 could help attract partnerships in climate-smart agriculture, agricultural research, sustainable value chains and nature-based solutions. Green Legacy: Mobilizing citizens for environmental restoration Ethiopia's climate resilience agenda also extends beyond technological interventions and infrastructure investment to community participation and environmental restoration. The Green Legacy Initiative, launched in 2019 under the leadership of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, stands among the country's most prominent examples of large-scale citizen mobilization around environmental protection. Explaining the philosophy behind the initiative, the Prime Minister said Ethiopia's development approach of Medemer brings citizens, institutions and resources together around shared national objectives. "Every year, millions of Ethiopians join in planting trees. Together, we have planted over 56 billion seedlings, restoring degraded land and expanding our forests," he said at COP31. The initiative has mobilized millions of citizens in tree planting, watershed development and environmental restoration, making environmental protection an increasingly visible part of national development efforts. Its significance, however, extends beyond the number of seedlings planted. The initiative contributes to soil conservation, water resource protection, biodiversity preservation and the broader objective of building a climate-resilient green economy. "The initiative has created jobs and improved livelihoods. Planting is now a family habit. It is teaching us to honor the land we inherit, to live in harmony with nature, and to care for what we leave to our children," the Prime Minister stated. These remarks highlight the social and economic dimensions of environmental restoration, particularly its contribution to employment, community participation and intergenerational responsibility. Environmental restoration also complements major infrastructure investments. Protecting watersheds and restoring degraded landscapes can help reduce soil erosion and sedimentation, contributing to the long-term sustainability of reservoirs and hydropower facilities, including the GERD. Through COP32, Ethiopia could demonstrate how community-led environmental restoration can complement infrastructure development, strengthen water security and support sustainable economic growth. At the same time, independently verifiable evidence of seedling survival rates, forest-cover expansion, restored land areas and measurable ecological improvements will be essential to demonstrating the initiative's long-term environmental impact. Building climate-resilient cities and promoting sustainable mobility Ethiopia's climate agenda is also increasingly extending into urban development. As cities expand, flooding, pollution, environmental degradation and pressure on public infrastructure are becoming more pressing challenges. In response, the government has been pursuing urban interventions that combine environmental protection with improved public spaces and living conditions. Prime Minister Abiy highlighted ongoing efforts to rehabilitate urban rivers, strengthen flood protection and develop accessible green spaces. "We are extending that work into our cities, building flood fences, cleaning polluted rivers, and turning their banks into parks and walkways where families gather and children play," he said. Such initiatives reflect the importance of climate-resilient urban planning, particularly as rapid urbanization increases exposure to flooding and environmental pressures. Ethiopia's transition towards cleaner transportation represents another dimension of its green development agenda. At COP31, the Prime Minister highlighted the country's decision to ban imports of petrol and diesel-powered vehicles as part of efforts to accelerate electric mobility. "Ethiopia is doing its part. We have banned imports of petrol and diesel cars as we switch to EVs," he said. The policy forms part of broader efforts to reduce dependence on imported fossil fuels, promote electric transportation and align the transport sector with the country's expanding clean-energy ambitions. It also demonstrates how domestic policy measures can support climate objectives while addressing economic priorities, including energy security and the country's import bill. These experiences provide further opportunities for Ethiopia to engage international partners on clean transportation, charging infrastructure, electric mobility technologies and sustainable urban development. COP32 and the wider economic opportunities for Ethiopia Beyond climate diplomacy and environmental priorities, hosting COP32 could generate substantial economic opportunities across several sectors. Thousands of international delegates, government officials, researchers, investors, journalists and representatives of international organizations are expected to travel to Addis Ababa, generating increased demand for accommodation, aviation, transportation, hospitality and other services. Ethiopian Airlines, hotels, tourism operators and local businesses could benefit from the increased international activity. The conference would also provide an exceptional platform to promote Ethiopia's cultural heritage, historical destinations and natural attractions to a global audience. More importantly, COP32 could strengthen the country's international profile and create opportunities for new bilateral relationships, investment agreements and strategic partnerships
ethiopia.summary: Ethiopia is leveraging its role as the host of COP32 in 2027 to enhance its diplomatic influence and advance Africa's climate agenda. By participating in COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, Ethiopia aims to forge partnerships, secure climate finance, and emphasize the continent's needs in global negotiations. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed highlighted the connection between climate action and economic policy, stressing that climate resilience is vital for Ethiopia's agricultural and hydropower-dependent economy. The country seeks to mobilize resources for renewable energy, sustainable agriculture, and climate-resilient infrastructure, while also promoting initiatives like the Africa Climate Innovation Compact. Ethiopia's hosting of COP32 is seen as a chance to strengthen Africa's negotiating position and showcase its potential as a leader in renewable energy solutions. The conference aims to shift the narrative from Africa as merely vulnerable to climate change to a continent rich in sustainable investment opportunities. Ethiopia's strategic approach emphasizes early action and accessible climate finance to bolster resilience and development. (158 words)

ethiopia.title: The Bone-Setters' Ward - How Ancient Healers Are Filling Ethiopia's Modern Healthcare Vacuum
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: The Bone-Setters' Ward - How Ancient Healers Are Filling Ethiopia's Modern Healthcare Vacuum - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: The Bone-Setters' Ward - How Ancient Healers Are Filling Ethiopia's Modern Healthcare Vacuum 13 November 2026 African Arguments analysis By Sleshi Teshome Kehali In a residential neighbourhood of Bahir Dar, in northwestern Ethiopia, patients visit the home of W/ro Birqe Yibre for help with injuries. Birqe, a traditional bone-setter known locally as a Wogesha, has practised for more than 20 years. One of her patients, Yidersal Mengistu, came with a painful right foot and a bruised big toe after kicking a stone while playing football. "I didn't go to the hospital. To be honest, I prefer the traditional way," Mengistu said. He explained that he had visited Birqe before for heel pain and believed her treatment had helped him. He also said she had treated him without charge on that earlier occasion. "If I recover fully this time, I will pay her," he said. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines For Birqe, payment depends partly on what patients can afford. She said people who have money typically pay between 150 and 200 Ethiopian birr, while she treats those who cannot pay without charging them. "If someone has no money, I treat them and tell them, 'Go on, go home,"' she said. "You cannot turn away poor people." A study of 836 people with a history of injury in Mecha district, published in BMC Complementary Medicine and Therapies , found that 46.05 per cent had used traditional bone-setting services. Social acceptance was the most commonly reported reason for seeking this care. The findings reflect the study population in Mecha district and should not be taken as a national estimate. For patients such as Mengistu, the decision is also shaped by personal experience and trust. But the treatment of fractures and other serious injuries can carry risks when patients delay seeking medical assessment. Knowing When to Refer Birqe said she distinguishes between injuries she believes she can treat and those that require hospital care. "I handle muscle pulls and minor dislocations," she said. "If someone comes with a serious, displaced bone or a deep fracture, I tell them plainly to go to the hospital. I don't try to touch it." She said she was concerned about practitioners who accept serious cases despite lacking the necessary skills to manage them. According to Birqe, some bone-setters bind injured limbs tightly with bamboo splints, locally known as Timaq, and continue treatment even when a patient's condition worsens. She said some eventually advise patients to seek hospital care only after several visits. "When parents bring me a child whose hand is already ruined, I tell them: 'Run to the hospital, I won't touch this,"' she said. Her account highlights a distinction within traditional practice: while Birqe says she refers serious injuries, she believes other practitioners take on cases beyond their abilities. These claims describe her experience and observations; establishing how widespread such practices are would require further evidence. A Crooked Arm Thomas Habtamu, a student living in Bahir Dar, said a fall during a neighbourhood football match injured his left forearm. Because of his family's financial difficulties, he did not go to a hospital and instead sought treatment from a local Wogesha. "The healer kept massaging it week after week, telling me to be patient," Habtamu recalled. He said the injury was close to the joint and that the treatment did not restore the arm to its normal position. "He told me that if I ever fell down and hurt the arm again in the future, he might be able to reset it then," Habtamu said. Habtamu has never had the arm examined at a hospital. He said his forearm remains visibly bent and that he struggles with activities such as push-ups, lifting heavy objects and prolonged gym exercise. He contrasted his experience with that of a friend who sustained a similar injury around the same time. According to Habtamu, his friend went to hospital, underwent an operation in which a metal plate was inserted, and recovered the use of his arm within about two months. The two accounts illustrate the different experiences the men reported. Without medical records or an examination, however, the precise nature of Habtamu's injury and the extent to which the treatment contributed to his current condition remain unconfirmed. What Happens When Fractures Are Not Properly Treated? At Tibebe Ghion Specialized Hospital in Bahir Dar, Dr Biruk Ferede, an orthopaedic specialist, said some patient's mistake natural bone healing for proof that a traditional treatment has worked. "An undisplaced fracture can heal naturally on its own; bone is living tissue that knits over time," he said. He warned that manipulating a displaced fracture or an injured joint without appropriate assessment can cause further problems. One possible complication is malunion, in which a fractured bone heals in an incorrect position. Dr. Biruk said correcting such injuries can require more complex surgery than treating them soon after they occur. He explained that surgeons may need to cut and realign a bone that has healed in the wrong position and secure it with plates. Stiffness in a nearby joint can make treatment more difficult, particularly when care has been delayed. Dr. Biruk also raised concerns about tightly applied traditional splints, especially when used on children. Swelling around an injured limb can increase pressure beneath a tight binding and compromise blood circulation. Severe cases may result in permanent tissue damage. He said children are particularly vulnerable because they may be unable to communicate the severity of their pain or remove a restrictive splint themselves. "Children cry continuously, but parents may assume the crying is just normal pain," he said. He described cases in which children arrived at hospital with severely damaged limbs and amputation was considered necessary. Trust, Access and Medical Care Dr. Biruk said social expectations can also influence treatment decisions. He recalled an incident involving a fifth-year medical student who sustained a fracture. According to the doctor, family members and neighbours took the student to a Wogesha before the student could decide where to seek care. "If an educated medical student faces that kind of pressure, what do you expect from ordinary citizens?" he asked. The incident, as recounted by Dr. Biruk, illustrates the influence that family and community expectations can have on decisions about treatment. It does not establish how frequently this happens, but it offers an example of how social pressure may affect an individual's choices even when formal medical care is familiar to them. Some health advocates have suggested providing traditional bone-setters with basic training to help them recognise serious injuries and refer patients to hospitals. Dr. Biruk is sceptical that short training can make practitioners safe to manage fractures. "Becoming an orthopaedic surgeon requires years of medical education and specialist training," he said. "You cannot turn someone into a safe trauma practitioner with short training." He argued that basic first-aid awareness should be available to the public, while suspected fractures and serious injuries should receive assessment from qualified medical professionals. Birqe's account, meanwhile, points to why some patients continue to seek help outside hospitals: she offers familiar care and says she does not turn away people who cannot pay. Habtamu's experience shows why a patient's decision about where to seek treatment can have lasting consequences. Their stories do not establish that all traditional bone-setters practise in the same way, or that every patient who visits one will suffer complications. They do, however, raise questions about how people assess injuries, what influences their choices and how quickly they can access appropriate medical care. For patients with suspected fractures, the challenge is to seek treatment that addresses the injury before complications develop. Understanding why people turn to traditional practitioners is part of that challenge, but so is ensuring that serious injuries receive timely medical attention. Research published in the Journal of Bone and Joint Surgery examined amputations associated with traditional bone-setting in southern Ethiopia. During an initial two-year retrospective review, researchers recorded 49 amputations, 25 of which were associated with gangrene following tight splintage by traditional bone-setters. After instructional courses were provided to 112 traditional healers and local health assistants, a subsequent two-year prospective study recorded 25 amputations, including seven associated with gangrene. The author concluded that educating traditional healers could help reduce amputations caused by gangrene. However, the findings come from a specific setting and period and should not be treated as a measure of the prevalence of these complications across Ethiopia. ethiopia.summary: In Bahir Dar, Ethiopia, traditional bone-setters like W/ro Birqe Yibre are increasingly sought after as modern healthcare remains inaccessible for many. Birqe, a Wogesha with over 20 years of experience, treats patients based on their ability to pay, often providing free care to those in need. A study indicated that nearly half of the surveyed individuals in the Mecha district had utilized traditional bone-setting services, primarily due to social acceptance and personal trust. However, the risks associated with delaying hospital care for serious injuries are significant. While Birqe refers complex cases to hospitals, some practitioners may mishandle severe injuries, leading to complications like malunion or permanent damage. Dr. Biruk Ferede, an orthopaedic specialist, emphasizes the need for public education on injury assessment and the importance of timely medical intervention. The ongoing reliance on traditional healers highlights the challenges in Ethiopia's healthcare system, necessitating a balance between traditional practices and formal medical care. (159 words)

ethiopia.title: Ethiopia's Green Legacy Showcases Commitment to Global Climate Action - Pmo Press Secretary
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia's Green Legacy Showcases Commitment to Global Climate Action - Pmo Press Secretary - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia's Green Legacy Showcases Commitment to Global Climate Action - Pmo Press Secretary 13 November 2026 Ethiopian News Agency (Addis Ababa) Addis Ababa — The Green Legacy Initiative stands as a testament to Ethiopia's commitment to combating climate change through large-scale afforestation, environmental conservation and sustainable development, Press Secretary for Office of the Prime Minister (PMO) Billene Seyoum said. Speaking at a briefing on Ethiopia's participation in the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, Türkiye, Billene highlighted the country's progress in environmental protection, renewable energy expansion and preparations to host COP32 in 2027. She disclosed that Ethiopia has planted more than 56 billion seedlings over the past eight years under the Green Legacy Initiative. The Press Secretary described this the flagship national programme as a major contribution to global efforts to mitigate climate change and restore degraded ecosystems. Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines Billene stressed, however, that the initiative's success should not be measured by the number of seedlings planted alone, but also by their survival, continued care and protection to ensure lasting environmental benefits. She called for broader public participation in environmental conservation, emphasizing that nurturing and protecting planted trees must become a shared responsibility across all sections of society. She also recalled Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's repeated calls for citizens to take an active role in caring for planted trees to maximize their long-term environmental and economic benefits. Turning to Ethiopia's clean energy transition, Billene highlighted the country's expanding investments in hydropower, wind and solar energy to meet growing domestic electricity demand while strengthening its capacity to supply power to regional markets. She cited ongoing wind and solar projects as evidence of Ethiopia's efforts to diversify its renewable energy mix and advance a sustainable energy future. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), she added, represents a major milestone in the country's renewable energy ambitions and electricity generation capacity. The landmark project will also be showcased at the Ethiopian Pavilion during COP31, she pointed out. Billene underscored that Ethiopia's investments in renewable energy, afforestation and environmental protection go beyond domestic development priorities, contributing to broader international efforts to address climate change and promote sustainable development. The briefing also highlighted Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's engagements at COP31, Ethiopia's preparations to host COP32 in 2027, and the country's plans to present its development achievements and climate action initiatives to the international community. Additionally, she discussed Ethiopia's investments in renewable energy, including hydropower, wind, and solar projects, to meet domestic electricity needs and enhance regional power supply. The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) is a key project in this transition. Billene reiterated that Ethiopia's environmental efforts contribute to global climate initiatives, while also preparing to showcase its achievements at COP32 in 2027.
